section_1.title: The Hook: Learning through Trial and Error
section_1.content: Introduce the core concept of a neural network as a series of adjustable 'knobs' (weights). Define 'learning' not as magic, but as the mathematical process of minimizing a mistake. Establish the goal: making the network's prediction match reality.
section_1.example: Imagine a robot dog named 'Bit'. Bit is shown a photo of a cat but barks 'Dog!'. To learn, Bit needs to know how wrong he was and which parts of his 'brain' caused the mistake.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Forward Pass & The Chain of Command
section_2.content: Explain how data flows from input to output. Visualize neurons as stations and weights as 'volume sliders' that amplify or dampen signals. Introduce the activation function as a 'gatekeeper'.
section_2.example: Input (Cat Pixels) -> Weight (Importance) -> Neuron (Summing up) -> Output (Prediction). If the 'Whiskers' weight is high, the signal for 'Cat' becomes stronger.

section_3.title: Defining the 'Ouch': The Loss Function
section_3.content: Introduce the 'Loss Function' (or Cost Function) as a mathematical ruler measuring the distance between the prediction and the truth. Use a parabolic graph to show the 'valley' of minimum error.
section_3.example: Bit predicted 0.9 (Dog) but the truth was 0.0 (Dog). The 'Ouch' factor (Loss) is the square of the difference: (0.9 - 0)^2 = 0.81. High loss means a big correction is needed.

section_4.title: The Blame Game: Intuitive Backpropagation
section_4.content: Explain the 'Chain Rule' through the lens of attribution. We move backward from the output error to the input, asking: 'How much did this specific knob contribute to the total error?' Use a reverse-flowing color gradient (e.g., red for high error contribution) to visualize the signal.
section_4.example: The output error flows back to the last layer of neurons. If a specific neuron was very active but led to the wrong answer, it gets more 'blame' (a higher gradient). This is like a manager tracing a factory error back to a specific machine.

section_5.title: The Adjustment: Gradient Descent
section_5.content: Introduce the 'Gradient' as a compass pointing toward the steepest increase in error. To improve, we move in the opposite direction. Explain 'Learning Rate' as the size of the step we take down the hill.
section_5.example: Visualizing a ball rolling down a foggy mountain. If the gradient says 'Up is North,' we take a small step South. We nudge the 'Whisker' knob slightly up and the 'Floppy Ear' knob slightly down.

section_6.title: Closing the Loop: Iteration
section_6.content: Summarize the cycle: Forward Pass (Predict) -> Calculate Loss (Measure) -> Backpropagate (Assign Blame) -> Update Weights (Correct). Emphasize that thousands of these tiny 'nudges' result in intelligence.
section_6.example: After 1,000 photos of cats and dogs, Bit’s knobs are perfectly tuned. Now, when he sees whiskers, the signal flows perfectly to the 'Cat' output. The robot dog has learned!
